items.title: Bulk Create and Update Mitigating Controls in SAP GRC Access Control
items.author: madhusap
items.text:
Introduction 
 Anyone who has worked on SAP GRC Access Control implementations will know the effort of creating and maintaining mitigating controls , especially when the same set must be loaded into several environments. The standard Mitigating Controls screen handles one control at a time. Each control needs an organisation, a business process and subprocess, an approver, monitors and the risks it mitigates. For a handful of controls this is fine. For a few hundred, it is slow and error prone. 
 For the manual steps, see this article on creating mitigation controls: https://community.sap.com/t5/financial-management-blog-posts-by-members/sap-grc-10-0-10-1-12-0-creation-of-mitigation-controls/ba-p/13257231 
 This post describes a custom ABAP report that creates or updates mitigating controls in bulk from an input file. It was built and tested on the following release: 

 Objective 
 Replicate the standard screen, but faster, without bypassing any standard GRC validations. 
 The report does not write to database tables directly. It calls the standard GRC classes and methods in the same sequence as the screen: open a session, lock the control, update, save, unlock. Standard authorisation checks, locking and change logs therefore behave exactly as they do for manual maintenance. The selection screen, file F4 help and logging follow the pattern of the standard report GRFN_MDUG. 
 Program Name The below screenshot shows the custom program ZR_WCE_MASS_MITICTRLS_CREATION , which is used to initiate the bulk mitigating-control creation/update process. Running the program opens the upload screen where the template file can be selected and processed. 

 Users choose a tab delimited or CSV file, set the delimiter, and run in one of two modes: 
 Test run: validates every record and reports what would be created or updated. Nothing is written. 
 Create / update run: writes the controls after a confirmation that names the system and client. 
 A control ID that does not exist is created. One that already exists is updated. 

 The Download Template button saves a ready to fill file. It has nine columns: 
 MIT_ID (control ID, up to 10 characters) 
 TITLE (up to 40 characters) 
 DESCRIPTION 
 ORG_UNIT (organisation name or object ID) 
 AC_BPROC (business process) 
 AC_BSUBPROC (business subprocess) 
 APPROVER 
 MONITORS (separated by semicolons) 
 RISK_IDS (separated by semicolons) 
 Selecting the file and running in Test run only mode allows users to specify the file format and delimiter and then run the process initially to identify any issues before committing the changes. 

 Validations 
 Every record is checked for column count, field lengths, mandatory fields and duplicate control IDs in the file. The organisation, business process and subprocess must exist, every risk must exist in the ruleset, and the approver and monitors must be valid SAP users. Inactive risks are skipped with a warning, and a record with no active risk left fails. All checks run for each record, so one pass shows everything wrong with it. 
 Organisation rule 
 Several organisation objects can carry the same name. The report uses the one whose Access Control owner list contains the approver and all monitors. If none does, the record fails with a message listing what was checked. Nothing is guessed. 
 Update behaviour 
 The file is the source of truth for the fields it carries: title, description, organisation, process, subprocess, approver, monitors and risks are replaced. Anything not in the file stays as it is. A control locked by another user fails with the standard lock message and is left untouched. 
 Results 
 Each record is saved on its own. A failed record is discarded and never affects the others. The result list shows one row per record with a status light, and a double click shows all its messages. Failures report the step that failed and the real GRC messages. 

 Where data is read and written 
 The report reads three tables directly with Open SQL: 
 USR02: confirms the approver and monitors are real users. 
 HRP1000: finds organisation objects by name or ID. 
 GRACSODRISK: confirms each risk exists and is active. 
 Everything else goes through standard classes: 
 Control data: CL_GRPC_API_CONTROL 
 Organisation owner list: CL_GRFN_API_EXT_AC_OWNER 
 Approver and monitors: CL_GRFN_API_EXT_AC_OWNER_CN 
 Risk link: CL_GRFN_API_EXT_AC_RISK (stored in HRT5320 by the API) 
 Process configuration: CL_GRAC_ERM_CONFIG 
 The persisted lock (GRFNLOCKOBJECT) is released through the standard unlock method. 
 Security 
 Front end file transfer is checked with S_GUI activity 61. Assign the report to an authorisation group (object S_PROGRAM) so only GRC administrators can run it. It uses no dynamic SQL, no native SQL and no server file access. File values are cleaned and length checked, text starting with =, + or @ is rejected to prevent spreadsheet formula injection, and run limits protect against oversized files. 
 Uploaded Mitigating Controls 
 The uploaded mitigating controls are shown in the Mitigating Controls work centre. The screen displays the control ID, title, and detailed control description, allowing users to review the controls created or updated through the bulk upload process. 

 Thank you for reading. I hope this program can help you in your GRC implementations to quickly create mitigating controls. 
 If you have questions, please drop a comment below. 
 You can also reach me directly at Maddysmail26@gmail.com whether it's a quick question, a deeper implementation challenge, or just a conversation about SAP. 
 Let's continue learning, sharing and building on each other's experience

items.title: AIF for cFiN - Basic (part 1) - Why Central Finance postings fail, and where SAP AIF fits in?
items.author: abhishek_singh1404_195
items.text:
Central Finance rejects a replicated document. Maybe the period is closed, a cost center is blocked, a value is mapped to the wrong target, or something technical went wrong. The error sits in AIF, and nobody knows who should touch it. 
 This post draws the line between four owners: finance, master data, mapping and the CFIN technical consultant. It follows an error from the monitor to the fix, then to the restart, and it covers the case where the right answer is to cancel the message instead.

items.title: SAP BTP Cockpit now introduces Scripting and Automation Preview panel
items.author: Yogananda
items.text:
Automate Everything: A Deep Dive into SAP BTP's Scripting & Automation Preview 
 Introduction 
 If you have ever set up an SAP BTP subaccount manually — clicking through the cockpit, filling in forms, waiting for confirmations — you know how repetitive and error-prone that process can be, especially at scale. SAP BTP has quietly introduced a game-changing feature right inside the BTP Cockpit: Scripting & Automation Preview . 
 This feature bridges the gap between point-and-click administration and true infrastructure-as-code, giving developers and platform engineers an instant script for every action they take in the cockpit — in SAP BTP CLI , Cloud Foundry CLI , and Terraform flavors. 
 What Is Scripting & Automation Preview? 
 Scripting & Automation Preview is a contextual code panel built directly into the SAP BTP Cockpit. For every page you are on — subaccount overview, entitlements, Cloud Foundry environments, service instances — the panel displays the equivalent SAP BTP CLI , Cloud Foundry CLI , and Terraform commands automatically. Crucially, it updates in real time as you navigate: no refresh, no manual lookup, no copy-pasting values from the UI into a docs page. 
 The panel is accessible via the <> icon in the top-right corner of the BTP Cockpit toolbar (see the screenshot below — it is highlighted in the navigation bar). Once activated, it docks at the bottom of the screen. As you move from one cockpit page to another, the panel silently updates its content to match your current context, making the transition from UI-based actions to scripted or infrastructure-as-code workflows completely frictionless — with no manual research required. 

 The Scripting & Automation Preview panel in the SAP BTP Cockpit, showing CLI commands auto-generated for a Global & subaccount 
 The Six Tabs — What Each One Gives You 
 The panel is organized into six tabs across three scripting paradigms, each serving a specific use case in the DevOps and platform engineering workflow: 
 SAP BTP CLI 
 1. CLI 
 The CLI tab generates ready-to-run SAP BTP CLI ( btp ) commands for the resource currently in view. This is the primary CLI for managing BTP platform resources — global accounts, subaccounts, entitlements, and environments. 
 For the "Mars" subaccount shown in the screenshot, it generates three commands automatically: 
 # Get the current subaccount 
btp get accounts/subaccount "10a...8a2f15" 

 # Create the subaccount 
btp create accounts/subaccount \
 --display-name "Mars" \
 --region "eu11" \
 --subdomain "mars" \
 --beta-enabled "true" 

 # Update the subaccount 
btp update accounts/subaccount "1...15" \
 --display-name "Mars" \
 --beta-enabled "true" 

 Each command block has a "View Documentation" link alongside it — so you can jump straight to the official BTP CLI reference for that specific command. No more hunting through docs to find the right flag. 
 2. CLI Setup 
 The CLI Setup tab provides the prerequisite setup commands needed before the BTP CLI commands will work — things like installing the BTP CLI, logging in to your global account, and targeting the right subaccount. This is invaluable for onboarding new team members or setting up CI/CD pipelines from scratch. 
 Cloud Foundry CLI 
 3. CF CLI 
 The CF CLI tab generates Cloud Foundry CLI ( cf ) commands for the current cockpit page. Where the BTP CLI covers platform-level resources (subaccounts, entitlements, service subscriptions), the CF CLI covers runtime-level resources: orgs, spaces, apps, services, buildpacks, routes, and environment variables. 
 For a Cloud Foundry environment page, the panel might surface commands like: 
 # Target the Cloud Foundry org and space 
cf login -a "https://api.cf.eu11.hana.ondemand.com" 
cf target -o "my-org" -s "dev" 

 # Create a Cloud Foundry space 
cf create-space "dev" -o "my-org" 

 This is particularly valuable because the cf command surface is vast, and remembering the exact syntax for service binding, role assignment, or environment variable management is non-trivial. The panel handles that for you. 
 4. CF CLI Setup 
 The CF CLI Setup tab provides the commands needed to install and authenticate the Cloud Foundry CLI — including the API endpoint specific to your BTP region — so a new pipeline or developer machine can be configured with a single copy-paste. 
 Terraform 
 5. Terraform 
 The Terraform tab generates a Terraform HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language) configuration block equivalent to the current cockpit state. This is the bridge between the visual cockpit and infrastructure-as-code: 
 resource "btp_subaccount" "mars" {
 display_name = "Mars"
 subdomain = "mars"
 region = "eu11"
 beta_enabled = true
} 
 With this output, you can bootstrap your Terraform codebase directly from the cockpit without having to manually author resource blocks from scratch. 
 6. Terraform Setup 
 The Terraform Setup tab gives you the provider configuration and backend setup code needed to get Terraform running with the SAP BTP Terraform Provider . It includes the required_providers block and authentication setup — removing all the boilerplate research. 
 A note on tabs visible in the screenshot: The screenshot shows four tabs — CLI, CLI Setup, Terraform, and Terraform Setup. The Cloud Foundry CLI tabs appear contextually when you navigate to a Cloud Foundry environment page within your subaccount. The full panel adapts its available tabs based on what resource type is currently in view. 
 Why This Feature Matters 
 For Platform Engineers: Shift Left on Automation 
 Historically, BTP Admins or teams would set up BTP resources manually in the cockpit during a project's early phases and only later "clean up" by writing CLI scripts or Terraform configs. The Scripting & Automation Preview collapses that timeline. You can write automation from day one — with zero risk of the script diverging from what was actually provisioned, because the cockpit generates it from the live resource state. 
 For Developers: No More CLI Reference Hunting 
 The BTP CLI is powerful but has hundreds of commands and flags. Remembering the exact syntax for btp create accounts/subaccount — including all the required and optional parameters — is a cognitive burden. With this feature, the cockpit tells you the exact command to run, pre-filled with the real values of your current resource. 
 For DevOps Teams: Reproducible Environments 
 One of the hardest problems in BTP operations is reproducibility. "Works in dev, doesn't work in prod" often traces back to configuration drift. When you can generate the exact Terraform or CLI script from a known-good environment, you get a reliable blueprint for spinning up identical environments elsewhere. 
 For Auditors and Compliance Teams 
 Every command the panel generates corresponds to a real API call against the BTP accounts service. Combined with the Open in Audit Log Viewer link visible in the subaccount overview, you have a complete trail from human intention → machine command → audit log. 
 A Real-World Scenario: Bootstrapping a New Subaccount 
 Let me walk through exactly how this feature speeds up a real task. 
 Scenario : You need to create a new "Production" subaccount mirroring the "Mars" dev subaccount, in the same region, with the same settings. 
 Old way (15–20 minutes): 
 Open BTP Cockpit. 
 Navigate to the global account. 
 Click "Create Subaccount", fill in the form. 
 Separately, open BTP CLI docs and find btp create accounts/subaccount . 
 Write the command manually, referring to the form values. 
 Copy the command into your runbook or automation script. 
 New way with Scripting & Automation Preview (2–3 minutes): 
 Open the "Mars" subaccount in BTP Cockpit. 
 Click the <> icon to open the Scripting & Automation panel. 
 Copy the Create Subaccount CLI command from the CLI tab. 
 Adjust --display-name and --subdomain for production. 
 Run or paste into your pipeline script. 
 The Terraform tab gives you an equivalent HCL block you can drop straight into your main.tf . 
 Beta Features: Why It's Enabled 
 Notice in the screenshot that Beta Features: Enabled is shown for the Mars subaccount. The Scripting & Automation Preview is currently in preview/beta status — you need beta features enabled at the subaccount level to access it. This is straightforward to enable via: 
 btp update accounts/subaccount <subaccount-id> --beta-enabled "true" 

 Ironically, the panel itself shows you this command once beta is enabled — self-referential and elegant. 
 Getting Started 
 Here's what you need to begin using Scripting & Automation Preview: 
 Step Action 
 1 Log in to SAP BTP Cockpit 
 2 Navigate to your target subaccount 
 3 Enable Beta Features in subaccount settings 
 4 Click the <> icon in the top-right toolbar 
 5 Navigate your resources — the panel updates automatically 
 6 Copy commands from CLI , Terraform , or their respective setup tabs 
 Current Scope and Limitations 
 As with any preview feature, there are things to be aware of: 
 Preview status means the generated scripts should be reviewed before being used in production pipelines — commands, flags, and Terraform resource schemas may evolve as the feature matures. 
 Coverage across resource types is expanding with each BTP Cockpit release. Some edge-case configurations may not yet have complete equivalents in all three scripting paradigms. 
 The panel's tabs adapt to context: BTP CLI tabs appear for subaccount/entitlement pages, CF CLI tabs appear for Cloud Foundry environment pages. Not all tab types are visible on every page — this is by design, not a gap. 
 Copy-paste is currently the primary integration mechanism. Direct export to a file or a Git repository would be a powerful next step. 
 What's Next? 
 The direction this feature points toward is clear: SAP wants every action in the BTP Cockpit to be scriptable by default . The logical next steps could include: 
 Session recording — capture a full sequence of cockpit actions as a single script or Terraform plan. 
 Export to file — download the generated scripts directly rather than copy-pasting. 
 CI/CD integration — push generated configs directly to a connected Git repository. 
 Drift detection — compare the live cockpit state against a stored Terraform state file and highlight differences. 
 Conclusion 
 Scripting & Automation Preview is one of those features that sounds simple but has significant implications for how teams manage BTP infrastructure. It removes friction from the shift to infrastructure-as-code, accelerates developer onboarding, and makes reproducibility a default rather than an afterthought. 
 The feature's core design principle is elegant: whatever page you are on, the cockpit tells you how to do it from the command line or in code — automatically, without you asking. SAP BTP CLI for platform resources. Cloud Foundry CLI for runtime resources. Terraform for everything you want to version-control and replay. The panel stays in sync as you navigate, so you never lose context. 
 If you are running SAP BTP with beta features enabled, open the <> panel the next time you configure a subaccount or set up a Cloud Foundry space. Within minutes, you will have ready-to-run CLI commands and Terraform blocks — generated from the live state of your environment, pre-filled with real values, and linked directly to the official documentation. 
 That is not just convenient. That is a fundamentally better way to operate cloud infrastructure.

items.title: SAP BTP Job Scheduling Service — Introducing New Job Type: Destination Job
items.author: Yogananda
items.text:
Introduction 
 SAP Job Scheduling Service on SAP Business Technology Platform (SAP BTP) is the backbone of automated, time-driven workloads for cloud-native applications. Whether you need to trigger a nightly data sync, execute a recurring business process, or run a long-running background task — the service has you covered, across both the Cloud Foundry and Kyma runtimes, through a unified REST API and a web-based dashboard. 
 Historically, the service offered two job types: 
 HTTP Jobs — Invoke an application's action endpoint over HTTP (synchronously or asynchronously) within your Cloud Foundry space or Kyma namespace. 
 CF Task Jobs — Execute long-running Cloud Foundry tasks bound to a specific application in your CF space. 
 These two types are powerful within their respective boundaries. But enterprise workloads rarely live in a single space or namespace. Applications on SAP BTP frequently need to integrate with external systems — partner APIs, SAP cloud services in other subaccounts, on-premise backends, or internet-reachable third-party services. Until now, bridging that gap required writing intermediary proxy code just to relay a scheduled call outward. 
 That changes with the new Destination Job type. 
 What Is a Destination Job? 
 A Destination Job is a new job type in SAP Job Scheduling Service that allows you to call external applications — applications that are not part of your Cloud Foundry space or Kyma namespace — on a defined schedule. 
 Instead of pointing to an internal action endpoint URL, a Destination Job resolves its target through the SAP Destination service . This means the entire connectivity and authentication chain — URL resolution, token handling, proxy routing, certificate management — is offloaded to a managed BTP service that you almost certainly already use across your landscape. 
 Important: Destination Jobs support only destinations created via the SAP Destination service . Ad hoc URLs or hardcoded endpoints are not supported for this job type. 
 For a full overview of how to create and manage destinations, refer to the official SAP documentation: Managing Destinations on the SAP Help Portal. 
 Why Destination Jobs Matter 
 Modern enterprise architectures on SAP BTP are composed of multiple runtimes, subaccounts, and external systems. Consider these common scenarios: 
 A Cloud Foundry application needs to trigger a scheduled process in an SAP S/4HANA Cloud system. 
 A Kyma microservice must push periodic data to a third-party SaaS platform via REST API. 
 An automated job needs to call a remote integration flow running in SAP Integration Suite. 
 A scheduled process must invoke a backend in a different CF space or subaccount using a destination configured at subaccount level. 
 In all these cases, the target application is outside the scheduler's own runtime boundary. Previously, you'd need to build and maintain an intermediate service to receive the job trigger, resolve the destination, and relay the call. With Destination Jobs, the scheduler handles this natively — no proxy layer, no extra middleware. 
 How It Works 
 Destination Jobs integrate directly with the SAP Destination service. Here is the execution flow: 
 SAP Job Scheduling Service
 │
 │ (at scheduled time)
 ▼
SAP Destination Service
 ├── Resolves destination by name
 ├── Retrieves target URL
 ├── Performs authentication flow
 │ (OAuth2, Basic, Client Cert, etc.)
 └── Returns connection details
 │
 ▼
External Application / API
 (outside CF space / Kyma namespace) 
 At the scheduled time, the Job Scheduling Service picks up the Destination Job. 
 It calls the SAP Destination service and resolves the named destination to a target URL and authentication token. 
 It then invokes the external application using the resolved connection. 
 Execution status and run logs are captured back in the Job Scheduling Service dashboard. 

 Prerequisites 
 Before creating a Destination Job, ensure the following are in place: 
 Requirement Details 
 SAP Job Scheduling Service instance A service instance must exist in your BTP subaccount (Cloud Foundry or Kyma). 
 SAP Destination service instance A Destination service instance must be created and accessible in the same subaccount. 
 Destination configured At least one destination must be created and configured via the SAP Destination service in the BTP cockpit. 
 Dashboard access You must have the SpaceDeveloper role (CF) or SAP_Job_Scheduling_Service_Admin role (Kyma) to access the dashboard. 
 Target application reachable The external application must be reachable from BTP using the configured destination (internet, Private Link, or on-premise via Connectivity service). 
 Supported Destination Methods 
 Destination Jobs support only destinations created via the SAP Destination service . The SAP Destination service offers several methods to connect to external systems, each suited to different security and connectivity requirements. You can choose from these when setting up your destination in the BTP cockpit: 
 Method Use Case 
 No Authentication Public APIs or internal endpoints that require no credentials. 
 Basic Authentication Username and password-protected services on the internet or on-premise. 
 Client Certificate Authentication Mutual TLS (mTLS) — internet or Private Link endpoints requiring a certificate. 
 OAuth2 Client Credentials Service-to-service integrations with OAuth2-protected APIs (most common for scheduled workloads). 
 OAuth2 JWT Bearer Token exchange flows where the calling service asserts an identity via JWT. 
 OAuth2 SAML Bearer Assertion SAML-based trust flows, commonly used with SAP systems. 
 OAuth2 User Token Exchange User context propagation within the same tenant. 
 Principal Propagation On-premise connectivity with user identity forwarding (requires SAP Connectivity service). 
 For a complete list and configuration guidance, see Managing Destinations on the SAP Help Portal. 
 How to Create a Destination Job via the Dashboard 
 The SAP Job Scheduling Service dashboard is your central hub for managing all job types, including the new Destination Job. Here is a step-by-step walkthrough. 
 Step 1 — Open the Job Scheduling Service Dashboard 
 You can access the dashboard in two ways: 
 Via SAP BTP Cockpit: 
 Log in to the SAP BTP Cockpit . 
 Navigate to your Subaccount → Services → Instances and Subscriptions . 
 Locate your Job Scheduling Service instance. 
 Click View Dashboard from the Actions menu. 
 Via Service Bindings (CF): 
 In your Cloud Foundry space, go to Service Instances . 
 Find the Job Scheduling Service instance. 
 Click the (Open Dashboard) icon in the Actions column. 
 Note: You must have the SpaceDeveloper role (CF) or the SAP_Job_Scheduling_Service_Admin role (Kyma) to access and manage jobs in the dashboard. 
 Step 2 — Navigate to Jobs 
 Once in the dashboard: 
 In the left navigation area, choose Jobs . 
 The Jobs overview lists all existing jobs, along with their type, status, and schedule details. 
 Choose Create Job to begin creating your new Destination Job. 

 Step 3 — Configure the Destination Job 
 In the Create Job dialog, fill in the following fields: 
 Field Description 
 Name A unique, descriptive name for your job (e.g., sync-external-crm-data ). 
 Job Type Select Destination Job from the available job types. 
 Destination Name Enter the name of the destination as it appears in the SAP Destination service (case-sensitive). 
 HTTP Method Select the HTTP method the job should use when calling the external application (e.g., GET , POST , PUT ). 
 Path / Endpoint Optionally specify a path relative to the destination's base URL (e.g., /api/v1/sync ). 
 Payload For POST / PUT methods, provide the request body to send to the external application. 
 Description A human-readable description of what the job does (optional but recommended). 
 Active Toggle to activate the job immediately upon creation. 
 Tip: Ensure the destination name you enter exactly matches the name defined in the SAP Destination service cockpit — including capitalisation and special characters. 
 Step 4 — Add a Schedule 
 A job without a schedule does not run. After creating the job: 
 Open the newly created job from the Jobs list. 
 Navigate to the Schedules tab. 
 Choose Create Schedule . 
 Configure your schedule using one of the supported formats: 
 Format Example Description 
 Cron expression 0 2 * * * Runs at 02:00 every day 
 Recurring interval PT1H (ISO 8601) Runs every 1 hour 
 Specific date/time 2026-12-01T06:00:00Z One-time execution 
 Human-readable repeat 1 hour Simple recurring format 
 Optionally, set a Start Date/Time and an End Date/Time to bound the schedule window. 
 Choose Create to save the schedule. 
 Step 5 — Monitor Execution and Logs 
 Once your Destination Job is active and scheduled: 
 In the dashboard, open the job and go to the Logs or Run Logs section. 
 Each schedule execution is recorded with its status ( SUCCESS , FAILED , RUNNING ) and timestamp. 
 Detailed logs help diagnose connectivity issues, authentication failures, or unexpected responses from the external application. 

 Tip: For production workloads, consider enabling SAP Cloud ALM integration from the dashboard's Actions menu to monitor your Destination Job's health alongside other operational data in SAP Cloud ALM. This integration was introduced in May 2025. 
 All Three Job Types — A Complete Comparison 
 Feature HTTP Job CF Task Job Destination Job 
 Target Internal app endpoint (URL) CF task in bound app External app via SAP Destination 
 Scope Within CF space / Kyma namespace Within CF space only Outside CF space / Kyma namespace 
 Target resolution Direct URL CF API SAP Destination service 
 Execution mode Sync or async Always async HTTP (via Destination) 
 Created via REST API Yes No (dashboard only) Yes 
 Destination service required No No Yes 
 Authentication handled by Application code CF runtime Destination service 
 Best for Internal API automation Long-running background tasks Cross-boundary external integrations 
 Use Cases 
 Here are real-world scenarios where Destination Jobs deliver the most value: 
 1. Cross-Subaccount Integration Trigger a scheduled process in a service deployed in a different BTP subaccount, using a subaccount-level destination that points to it. 
 2. Periodic S/4HANA Cloud Sync Schedule a daily job to call an SAP S/4HANA Cloud OData service — authenticated via OAuth2 SAML Bearer — to push or pull business data without maintaining a proxy application. 
 3. Third-Party API Automation Call an external SaaS platform's REST API on a schedule (e.g., a marketing automation tool or a logistics tracking API), using OAuth2 Client Credentials for service-to-service authentication. 
 4. SAP Integration Suite Triggering Trigger an iFlow in SAP Integration Suite at a scheduled time, using a destination configured with the relevant endpoint and credentials. 
 5. On-Premise Backend Calls Invoke an on-premise backend system (via SAP Connectivity service and Cloud Connector) at a defined interval — the destination handles proxy routing transparently. 
 Best Practices 
 Name destinations clearly — Use descriptive, environment-specific names (e.g., s4hana-prod-odata , crm-api-staging ) so jobs are easy to audit. 
 Prefer OAuth2 Client Credentials for automated, unattended service-to-service calls — it is the most suitable authentication type for scheduled workloads. 
 Test your destination first — Use the Check Connection feature in the BTP Destination cockpit to validate the destination before creating the job. 
 Use recurring schedules over one-time schedules — SAP Job Scheduling Service deletes one-time schedules that have not run within the last 30 days (as of May 2025). 
 Enable SAP Cloud ALM monitoring — For business-critical Destination Jobs, activate Cloud ALM integration to get visibility into execution health. 
 Secure your payloads — Avoid embedding sensitive data in job payloads. Use destination

items.title: SAP Joule Work at SAP TechEd Berlin 2026: Redefining the Future of Work with Agentic AI
items.author: RanjeetKr
items.text:
How SAP is transforming enterprise productivity through an AI-native experience, intelligent agents, connected applications, and autonomous business execution. 
 The way we interact with enterprise software is about to change significantly. 
 For decades, employees have worked across multiple business applications, switching between screens, searching for information, navigating workflows, and coordinating activities across different departments. Even with automation and digital transformation, completing a business task often requires interaction with multiple systems. 
 But what if employees could simply describe what they want to accomplish, and AI could understand the objective, identify the required information, coordinate the relevant agents, and help complete the work? 
 This is the vision behind SAP Joule Work . 
 At SAP TechEd Berlin 2026, SAP announced significant advancements in Joule Work, demonstrating how enterprise AI is evolving beyond traditional conversational assistants toward intelligent, context-aware, and agent-driven business execution. 
 The announcement represents an important shift in SAP's user experience strategy: moving from application-centric interactions to an AI-native experience where business users can focus on outcomes rather than navigating individual applications. 
 Let's explore what is new in SAP Joule Work and why it matters for the future of enterprise productivity. 
 1. What Is SAP Joule Work? 
 SAP Joule Work is SAP's AI-powered work experience designed to bring business applications, AI assistants, and intelligent agents together through a unified interface. 
 Instead of interacting with every application independently, employees can use Joule Work as a central starting point for their daily business activities. 
 Users can express their requirements in natural language, interact with AI assistants, access relevant business information, and work with agents that help coordinate activities across connected enterprise systems. 
 The key idea is simple: 
 Don't make employees navigate the business. Let AI help employees get business work done. 
 SAP is positioning Joule Work as a new way of experiencing enterprise software, bringing intelligence and business execution closer to where employees actually work. 
 2. A Completely Redesigned AI-Native User Experience 
 One of the major announcements at SAP TechEd Berlin 2026 is the redesigned Joule Work experience. 
 SAP has reimagined the user experience around a unified entry point, making it more intuitive to interact with business applications and AI capabilities. 
 The new experience brings together: 

 SAP business applications. 

 Microsoft 365. 

 Claude Cowork. 

 Glean. 

 ServiceNow. 

 SAP Joule Assistants and Joule Agents. 
 This is particularly interesting because enterprise employees rarely work within a single application ecosystem. 
 For example, a business user might need information from SAP S/4HANA, collaborate through Microsoft 365, retrieve organizational knowledge from Glean, and coordinate activities through ServiceNow. 
 Joule Work aims to bring these experiences together rather than forcing employees to continuously switch between different applications. 
 Another important capability is its ability to remember user preferences and context from previous interactions, allowing the experience to adapt to individual working patterns. 
 The business impact: A more consistent employee experience, reduced application switching, and easier access to business information and AI capabilities. 
 3. Conversations and Spaces: Two Important Ways of Working with Joule SAP TechEd highlighted two important elements of the Joule Work experience: Conversations and Spaces. 
 Conversations – Interact with Enterprise AI Naturally 
 Conversations provide a natural-language interface for interacting with Joule. 
 Users can ask questions, request information, seek recommendations, and engage with assistants and agents to accomplish business tasks. 
 For example: 
 "Show me the latest sales performance, identify the regions that are below target, and summarize the key reasons for the decline." 
 Rather than manually navigating multiple reports, users can interact with Joule through a conversational experience to explore business information and obtain relevant insights. 
 The objective is to make enterprise intelligence accessible through natural interactions. 
 Spaces – Bring Business Information Together 
 Spaces provide a collaborative experience where information can be brought together into interactive, reusable work environments. 
 Instead of keeping business information scattered across conversations and applications, users can work with contextual information and interactive applications within a shared space. 
 For example, a sales team could use a dedicated space to bring together: 

 Sales performance information. 

 Customer account details. 

 Pipeline insights. 

 Business recommendations. 

 Relevant applications and workflows. 
 This creates a more structured way to collaborate around specific business objectives. 
 Why this matters: Conversations help employees interact with AI, while Spaces help organize information and work around business outcomes. 
 4. Agentic Thinking: Moving from Answering Questions to Completing Complex Workflows 
 This is arguably one of the most important advancements announced for Joule Work at SAP TechEd Berlin 2026. 
 Traditional AI assistants typically respond to individual prompts or perform predefined tasks. 
 However, enterprise business processes are rarely simple. A single business objective can involve multiple systems, data sources, departments, and decision points.

items.title: Scalable and Reliable Large-Volume Data Synchronization Using SAP Integration Suite Pipeline Orchest
items.author: sajith_p
items.text:
Introduction 
 Organisations frequently need to synchronise large volumes of business data, such as master data, transactional records, financial information, and order data, between enterprise systems. Such integrations must be designed to process high data volumes efficiently while ensuring reliability, recover-ability, and minimal impact on source and target system performance. 
 This article describes an orchestration-based synchronisation framework built using SAP Integration Suite . The solution leverages JMS queues, pipeline integration flows, and parallel processing principles to transfer large datasets reliably and efficiently between source and target systems. 
 In this use case, the source system contains master data records that need to be synchronised with a target system without impacting operational performance. 
 The source system exposes APIs that provide the following capabilities: 
 Retrieve the total number of records available for synchronisation. 
 Retrieve a specific set of records based on page number and page size for a given date range. 
 By utilising SAP Integration Suite as the orchestration layer, large datasets can be split into manageable batches and processed independently, enabling scalability, fault tolerance, and efficient resource utilisation. 
 High-Level Solution Architecture 
 Process Flow Overview 
 Initiation: Scheduled Trigger 
 The synchronisation process begins with a scheduler that triggers the workflow at predefined intervals based on business requirements. 
 Once triggered, a message is placed into an initial JMS queue. This design provides decoupling between process stages and ensures message persistence. In the event of temporary connectivity failures or unexpected processing issues, the message remains available for automatic retry and reprocessing. 
 Key Benefits 
 Scheduled execution 
 Reliable message persistence 
 Automatic recovery from transient failures 
 Decoupled processing architecture 

 Planning: Determine Processing Scope and Create Jobs 
 After the workflow is initiated, the planning phase identifies the volume of data that must be synchronised. 
 During this step: 
 The source system API is invoked to retrieve the total record count. 
 The total number of pages is calculated based on the configured page size. 
 Required processing parameters are generated, including page number and page size. 
 A separate job message is created for each page of records. 
 All generated jobs are placed into a JMS queue for execution. 
 This approach converts a large synchronisation activity into multiple smaller and independently executable jobs. 
 Example 
 If: 
 Total Records = 1,000,000 
 Page Size = 10,000 
 Then: 
 Total Jobs = 100 
 Each job is responsible for processing one page of records. 
 Key Benefits 
 Workload distribution 
 Improved scalability 
 Independent processing of batches 
 Better system resource management 

 Execute Jobs from the Queue 
 Once jobs are available in the JMS queue, the execution flow starts processing them immediately. 
 For each job: 
 The corresponding message is consumed from the JMS queue. 
 The source API is called using the assigned page number and page size. 
 The requested batch of records is retrieved. 
 Using JMS as the processing backbone provides resilience against temporary API failures. If connectivity issues occur during execution, the message remains available for retry according to the configured retry mechanism. 
 Key Benefits 
 Reliable batch processing 
 Automatic retries 
 Failure isolation 
 Parallel execution capability 

 Retrieve Records and Deliver to the Target System 
 After successfully retrieving a batch of records from the source system, the data is forwarded to the target system through the SAP Integration Suite pipeline framework. 
 The processing utilises: 
 Pipeline Generic Step 06 – Outbound Processing 
 Pipeline Generic Step 08 – XI Outbound Processing 
 Step 06 provides built-in retry capabilities and reliability handling. If message delivery fails during Step 08 processing, the framework automatically retries transmission based on the configured retry settings. 
 This layered design ensures guaranteed delivery while maintaining high throughput for large volumes of data. 
 Key Benefits 
 Reliable target system delivery 
 Automatic retry handling 
 Reduced data loss risk 
 Standardised outbound processing framework 
 Solution Benefits 
 The proposed orchestration pattern provides several advantages for enterprise-scale integrations: 
 Scalability 
 Large datasets are divided into smaller processing units, enabling efficient handling of millions of records. 
 Performance Optimisation 
 Paginated data retrieval minimises load on the source system while reducing memory consumption within the integration platform. 
 Reliability 
 JMS-based processing ensures message persistence and recovery from temporary failures. 
 Parallel Processing 
 Multiple jobs can be processed simultaneously, significantly reducing overall synchronisation time. 
 Re-usability 
 The framework can be reused for synchronising: 
 Master Data 
 Order Data 
 Financial Data 
 Customer Data 
 Product Data 
 Transactional Records 
 Monitoring and Support 
 Each job represents an individual processing unit, simplifying operational monitoring, troubleshooting, and error recovery. 
 Conclusion 
 By combining SAP Integration Suite Pipeline Flows , JMS queues , and pagination-based processing , organisations can build a scale able and resilient synchronisation framework capable of handling high-volume data transfers efficiently. The solution minimises dependency on source system performance, provides built-in recovery mechanisms, supports parallel processing, and ensures reliable delivery to downstream applications. 
 This orchestration pattern serves as a reusable enterprise integration blueprint for synchronising large-scale master data, transactional data, financial records, and other business-critical information across heterogeneous systems.

items.title: CDS View Extensions in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition: Architecture, Tools, and What Matters
items.author: YashManjunath1
items.text:
***Applies to: SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition 2023 FPS01 and later. CDS extension mechanics apply from S/4HANA 1909 onwards; the Joule connectivity described here requires 2023 FPS01+*** 
 Part 1 of 2 | Series: Your SAP S/4HANA Data Model Is Your AI Strategy 
 Picture this scenario. As part of an SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition transformation project, your company has just enabled Joule on the SAP Fiori Launchpad. The demo has gone well. The finance lead is keen. Within the first week she asks: "Can Joule tell me the margin by our internal product tier classification?" 
 The answer is it cannot. Not because Joule can’t surface it, but because your product tier classification has been sitting in a Z-table since the SAP ERP days and was never added to any CDS view. From where Joule sits, that data does not exist. The same gap is blocking the OData API your integration team wants to expose. The same gap is blocking the SAC model your analytics team is trying to build. 
 One missing CDS extension. Three blocked workstreams. 
 That is the argument for getting CDS extensions right. Not one platform. All of them. 
 Supporting customers in my role as SAP S/4HANA RIG solution architect, I see this pattern on almost every transformation engagement and it rarely arrives alone. 
 Now picture the procurement lead sends a different request that same week: "Can we get planned delivery time into the purchasing analytics dashboard?" This one looks identical from the outside - another field Joule and SAC cannot see - but the cause is different. Planned delivery time already exists in SAP’s database. It is standard SAP data that simply has not been promoted to any released CDS view. No Z-table, no custom logic, but the fix is not the same either. 
 Two situations. Same symptom. Different cause. Different path. Let's work through both. 
 The SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition Context 
 In SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, SAP manages the HANA database, application server, and OS layers on hyperscaler or SAP’s own infrastructure. You own the application configuration, the transport landscape, and the extension estate. That split matters more than it sounds. 
 The release rhythm is: a base release every two years (S/4HANA 2023, 2025, 2027), Feature Pack Stacks every six months within a base release, delivering incremental innovations, and Support Pack Stacks after mainstream cutover, carrying only fixes. Mainstream maintenance runs seven years per base release. Under RISE with SAP, SAP executes the upgrade; you own the readiness work and the cutover decision. 
 In practice, that means upgrade preparation sits on your plate, and the quality of your extension determines how much of that preparation is analysis versus remediation. 
 Here is what upgrade readiness actually means for extensions. SAP runs the Software Update Manager (SUM) against your development system. As part of that process, ABAP activation checks run against every object in the customer namespace. Any extension that references an internal SAP object that has changed, which can be a view structure, a table field, or an association cardinality, will throw an activation error. Those errors block the transport chain. You cannot promote to QA or production until every activation failure in the development system is resolved, re-tested and re-transported. On a program with 50–100 custom extension objects, even three or four failures, you can add hours to days to a cutover window that is usually already tight. 
 The mechanism that prevents this is the C1 release contract. When SAP marks a CDS view as C1-released, it is a formal architectural commitment: the view's interface, its field names, types, and association signatures, will not change in ways that break downstream consumers. If your extension targets a C1-released view using EXTEND VIEW ENTITY, SAP owns the upgrade compatibility. If you've extended an unreleased view, used a Z-copy of a standard view, or written Classic ABAP that reads internal table structures directly, there is no contract and no guarantee. The ABAP Test Cockpit (ATC) will tell you how exposed you are; running it against your extension estate before each FPS is not optional, it's the earliest point at which you find out what needs to be fixed. 
 On-premise teams have exactly the same structural problem. The difference is that on-premise teams control the upgrade schedule and can defer it. In SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, that deferral option is limited; you stay current, or you fall out of mainstream maintenance. That is why the extension quality conversation that on-premise programs have been able to postpone tends to arrive earlier and more urgently for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition. 
 The Extensibility Stack: Where CDS Extensions Fit 
 SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition supports the full SAP extensibility portfolio. Understanding where CDS extensions sit within it matters before choosing your approach. 

 CDS view extensions, written as EXTEND VIEW ENTITY in ADT, sit in the Developer In-App tier. When targeting C1-released views, they are Level A: ABAP Cloud compliant and fully upgrade-safe. 
 One practical note specific to SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition: in a system configured with the ABAP Cloud language version, the compiler will reject references to unreleased objects . This is not a warning; it is a build failure. That enforcement mechanism is one of the more useful guardrails the platform provides. 
 Clean Core, Release Contracts, and Upgrade Safety 
 The A–D Classification 
 SAP's Clean Core framework maps to something concrete: whether your extension object activates cleanly after an upgrade without manual intervention. 

 Level 
 What it means 
 CDS extensions land here when... 

 A 
 ABAP Cloud compliant, released objects only 
 Targeting C1/C0-released views with EXTEND VIEW ENTITY 

 B 
 Stable interfaces, not fully cloud-ready 
 Extending views with partial release contracts 

 C 
 References internal SAP artifacts 
 Using unreleased views or internal objects 

 D 
 Direct modification of SAP standard 
 Not appropriate 

 Level A costs upfront discipline — checking release contracts, following the bottom-up propagation pattern, using the right syntax. That investment is front-loaded: a few extra steps at build time that translate into a quieter, lower-risk upgrade cycle. Level C and D extensions tend to surface at upgrade time as activation failures that need to be resolved before cutover. 
 Release Contracts 
 Before extending any CDS view, check its release contract. This is the formal binding between SAP and you on interface stability. 

 Contract 
 Name 
 What it means 
 What it enables 

 C0 
 Extend 
 Stability at defined extension points only. Has two visibility scopes: Use in Key User Apps or Use in Cloud Development — or both 
 CDS view extensions, append structures, BAdIs. Use in Key User Apps scope makes the view available in Custom Fields & Logic (F1481) and SCFD_REGISTRY tools 

 C1 
 Use System-Internally 
 Stable public interface guaranteed for use within the ABAP system. SAP will not change the interface in ways that break downstream consumers after an upgrade 
 Using the view as a data source in custom ABAP development within the same system 

 C2 
 Use as Remote API 
 Stable public interface guaranteed for use outside the ABAP system 
 Consuming the view via OData, remote function calls, or external API clients 

 No contract / internal 
 Unreleased 
 No stability guarantee — SAP can change or remove the object without notice 
 Nothing. Referencing these places your extension at Level C or D in the clean core classification 
 In ADT, open the target view and navigate to the API State tab. A C1 or C0 contract means SAP has committed to not changing the interface in ways that break extensions. @vdm .lifecycle.contract.type: #PUBLIC_LOCAL_API is a further contract type indicating a stable, released public interface — also safe to build on. 
 The Virtual Data Model: Your Extension Target 
 SAP's Virtual Data Model is a semantic stack with deliberate layering: The rule that matters most: extend at the lowest layer where the data lives and let it propagate up. If you only extend the consumption view, the OData service bound to the interface view won't see your field. If you extend the interface view, every consumer up the stack including OData, SAC, Fiori, Joule inherits it automatically. 
 You can see this layering live in the Fiori View Browser app (F2170). Search for I_PurchaseOrderItemAPI01, which is the view used in the code examples throughout this post. The results list shows its VDM View Type as Basic , confirming this is the interface layer: above the physical database, below the consumption views. This is the layer your extension targets. 

 In ADT, the view type is declared explicitly on every SAP-delivered VDM view via @vdm .viewType: #BASIC, #COMPOSITE, or #CONSUMPTION. This annotation drives behaviour in SAC, Embedded Analytics, and Fiori Elements, and tells you which layer you're working with before writing a single line of extension code. 

 Never extend P_* (private) views: no release contract, subject to change by SAP without notice. 
 Two Kinds of Data Gap 
 Two distinct situations produce the same symptom - a consumer that cannot find the data it needs. Diagnosing which one you are dealing with determines your path. 
 Gap 1: A Standard SAP Field Not Yet Exposed 
 The field exists in a standard SAP table, such as EKPO, MARA, LFA1, VBAP, but no released CDS view has ever selected it. This is more common than expected. SAP has exposed the majority of high-traffic fields through released views, but the long tail of table columns that matter to specific business scenarios is substantial. 
 First step: confirm with Alternative Search in View Browser (F2170) 
 Before concluding a field is unavailable, use the Alternative Search function. Open the View Browser (F2170), switch to the Alternative Search tab, and enter the table name and field name. This searches across all released CDS views for any that read that field from that table — including views you would not have found by name. 

 If no results carry the Released status, even if internal views reference the field, it is not accessible through any stable CDS interface. PLIFZ returns 86 views in this search shown above. None are Released. From Joule, SAC, or any OData client, this field does not exist. 
 Once confirmed, three paths forward in clean core preference order: 
 Option 1 — Key User path (cleanest) 
 Check whether the field's business context is available in the Custom Fields app (F1481). If it is, add the field as a key user extension. SAP handles CDS propagation and OData registration automatically. No developer code required and the result is Level A clean core. 
 Option 2 — Wrapper view (developer path) 
 If the key user path is not available, build a minimal custom CDS view that reads the fields directly from the SAP standard table, then extend the released interface view with an association to this wrapper. The wrapper reads unreleased SAP table structures — Level C in the clean core model. It works and can be made stable, but it carries an upgrade risk if SAP restructures the underlying table. Document it explicitly, add the base table to your Simplification List checks before each FPS and track it as technical debt until SAP delivers a clean release. 
 Note on ABAP Cloud mode: In an SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition system configured with ABAP Cloud language version, direct access to unreleased tables like EKPO will be rejected at compile time. Option 1 or Option 3 are the only supported paths in that configuration. 
 -- Wrapper view: reads unreleased SAP table directly (Level C in clean core) 
 -- Only build this after confirming the field is not already exposed 
 -- using Alternative Search in View Browser (F2170) 

 Option 3 — Request SAP to release the field

items.title: S4/HANA Cloud Private Edition (008) - APサーバからお客様のCIFSサーバ上の共有フォルダをマウントする方法
items.author: KevinYin
items.text:
SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Editionにおいて、APサーバからCIFSを利用し、お客様側のオンプレミス環境、またはお客様所有のCloud上のCIFSサーバ上のファイルへアクセスする方法についてご紹介いたします。 
 構成を整理いたしますと、以下のとおりとなります。 
 RISE側のAPサーバ: CIFSクライアント 

 お客様オンプレミス/お客様所有のCloud上のサーバ: CIFSサーバ 
 ご利用するService Request(以下、SR)テンプレートは、下記のとおりでございます。 
 SRテンプレート: Mount CIFS (aka Samba) shares 
 SRを起票される前に、下記の前提条件をご確認いただけますようお願いいたします。 
 RISE上のAPサーバからのみ、お客様所有のCIFSサーバをマウントできること(HANAサーバでのCIFSマウントは許可されておりません)。そのため、SRを作成される際は、SIDとしてAPサーバをご選択いただくこととなります。 
 RISE上のAPサーバと、お客様オンプレミス/お客様所有のCloud上のサーバ間でネットワーク通信が可能であること。 
 RISE側のAP(CIFSクライアント)から、CIFSサーバのポート139または445へアクセスできること(現状は、基本的にポート445が使用されます)。 
 CIFSマウントポイントの数は、1台のAPサーバ上で5つまでとなるよう設計いただくことを推奨いたします。 
 以下では、現時点で提供されている4つの"CIFS Operations"をもとにご説明いたします。 
 Create: Mount new customer CIFS shares on Linux hosts 
 Modify: Unmounts existing CIFS shares and Remount with modified details 
 Remount: Unmount and remount existing CIFS shares (without modifications) 
 Unmount: Unmount or cleanup existing CIFS shares 

 新規CIFSマウントの作成 

 新規でCIFSマウントポイントを作成する場合に利用いたします。 
 下記は、CIFSサーバ10.218.3.20の共有名sharenameを、該当サーバの/mnt/smbshareにマウントする例でございます。 

 Customer Domain Name : "CIFS User Name"でご指定いただくユーザがドメイン上に存在する場合は、ドメイン名をご指定ください。それ以外の場合はWORKGROUPとなります。 
 CIFS Share Name : 共有名をご指定ください。例えば、あるフォルダに対して共有設定を実施した後に設定した共有名となります。 
 CIFS User Name : CIFSクライアントからCIFSサーバへアクセスする際のユーザ名となります。 
 Is PASSWORD updated in Customer Logon Depot?: CIFSユーザのパスワードをLogon Depotに保存のうえ、チェックを入れてください。ご不明な場合は、SAP Notes 1773689をご参照ください。 
 Target Hostname(s) : RISE側のAPサーバのホスト名をご指定ください。複数のご指定が可能です。 
 Checking PORT access to CIFS Server : "TCP ports 445/139 are reachable, ready to proceed"と表示されることをご確認ください。お客様側で、RISE側のAPサーバからCIFSサーバの139または445ポートへのアクセスを許可いただく必要がございます。 
 Target Mount Point : RISE側APサーバにて、CIFSマウントポイントとなるディレクトリをご指定ください。免責事項に記載のある/install、/tmpなどの配下のディレクトリは利用しないようお願いいたします。 
 Mount Point permissions : 必須項目ではなく、デフォルトのパーミッションは775となります。必要に応じてご指定ください。 
 Share Owner : 必須項目ではなく、デフォルトのユーザグループはsidadm:sapsysとなります。通常は変更いただく必要はございませんが、特定の要件がある場合はご指定ください。 

 CIFSマウントの設定変更 

 既存のCIFSマウントの設定を変更する場合に利用いたします。 
 CIFSマウント変更の項目は、"Select entity to Modify"パラメータのダイアログボックスからご確認いただけます。下記は、現時点で選択可能な変更項目でございます。 
 CIFS Server details: Customer CIFS server details (ex. IP, FQDN, etc.) 
 Domain Name: Customer side Domain name of the CIFS server 
 CIFS Share Name: Customer side exported CIFS share name 
 CIFS user name: Customer side CIFS user name 
 CIFS password: Customer side CIFS password 
 ECS side Mount point: Modify CIFS mount point on SAP ECS host 
 Share permissions: Modify CIFS mount point permissions on SAP ECS host 
 Change share owner: Modify CIFS mount point owner on SAP ECS host 
 下記は、CIFSサーバへの接続時のパスワードを変更するSRを例としております。 

 CIFS Operations : Modify 
 Select entity to Modify : CIFS password 
 Is PASSWORD updated in Customer Logon Depot? : 変更後のパスワードをCustomer Logon Depotにメンテナンスしたうえで、チェックを入れてください。 
 Target Hostname(s) : CIFSクライアントとして稼働しているRISE上のAPサーバのホスト名をご指定ください(複数のホストをご指定いただけます)。 
 Target Mount Point : RISE上のAPサーバ上のマウントポイントをご指定ください。 
 CIFS mount point? : 上記のすべての項目の入力が完了しましたら、選択項目をクリックし、"Valid CIFS mount, good to preceed"が表示されることをご確認のうえ、クリックしてください。万が一、すべての項目を正しく入力しているにもかかわらず、"Valid CIFS mount, good to preceed"が表示されない場合は、RISEの担当者までご連絡ください。 

 CIFSマウントポイントの再マウント(設定変更なし) 

 既存のCIFSマウントを再マウント(アンマウント/マウント)する場合に利用いたします。 
 下記は、対象サーバ上のCIFSマウントポイント /mnt/smbshare の再マウント依頼の例でございます。 

 CIFS Operations : Remount 
 Target Hostname(s) : 対象サーバのホスト名をリストからご選択ください。 
 Target Mount Point: 該当サーバ上でのCIFSマウントポイントをご入力ください。大文字・小文字を含め、正確にご入力いただく必要がございます。 
 CIFS mount point? : 上記のすべての項目の入力が完了しましたら、選択項目をクリックし、"Valid CIFS mount, good to preceed"が表示されることをご確認のうえ、クリックしてください。万が一、すべての項目を正しく入力しているにもかかわらず、"Valid CIFS mount, good to preceed"が表示されない場合は、RISEの担当者までご連絡ください。 

 CIFSマウントポイントのアンマウント 

 CIFSマウントをアンマウントする場合に利用いたします。 
 下記は、対象サーバ上のCIFSマウントポイント /mnt/smbshare のアンマウント依頼の例でございます。 

 CIFS Operations : Unmount

items.title: How India Drives SAP’s AI Future
items.author: Alexa MacDonald
items.text:
India is emerging as the epicenter of SAP’s plans to build the Autonomous Enterprise. Few could have imagined this in 1998, when SAP opened its first office in Bengaluru and the location was little more than a back-office supporting the company’s headquarters in Walldorf, Germany. 

 Those days have long since been lost to history. 

 From a single building in Bengaluru, SAP’s presence in India has expanded across the country, transforming a small operation into one of SAP’s most important global innovation hubs. Today, more than 18,000 employees are on the payroll, making it SAP’s second largest location. 

 SAP’s presence in the country has two closely connected dimensions: SAP India, led by Manish Prasad, and SAP Labs India, led by Sindhu Gangadharan. 
 At SAP Labs India, innovation meets impact and ideas turn into intelligent enterprise solutions for the world 

 Learn more 

 SAP India is a regional business organization serving India, Sri Lanka, and Bangladesh. With locations in Bengaluru, Delhi, Hyderabad, Gurugram, Mumbai, and Pune, SAP Labs India drives product development and innovation for SAP solutions used worldwide. 

 SAP’s commitment and trust in SAP Labs India to deliver innovation is evident with the opening of SAP Labs India Innovation Park, located in Bengaluru, India’s top startup hub . Inaugurated in August 2025, this €194 million investment is SAP’s largest research and development hub outside of Germany and can accommodate an additional 15,000 employees. 

 From local solutions to global impact 

 Solving local challenges and then scaling the solutions globally has become a hallmark of SAP Labs India. Teams working to help customers navigate India’s complex tax reporting requirements laid the foundation of SAP Document and Reporting Compliance. Today, this solution serves customers in more than 50 countries. 

 That pattern of turning local expertise into global product innovation is now visible in SAP’s AI strategy. 

 With Sudhakar Singh, who leads the AI Security office, and the global head of engineering for Joule and head of SAP Business AI, Rahul Lodhe, both based at SAP Labs India, the location plays a visible role in shaping the agenda for the Autonomous Enterprise. 

 Teams in India engineered Joule , an AI solution grounded in SAP’s business data and context and integrated across SAP and non-SAP systems. Accessed via a conversational interface, Joule has evolved from a copilot and now orchestrates background AI capabilities and Joule Agents. 

 One example is the Data Product Creation Agent, designed to help  SAP Business Data Cloud users overcome the lack of quality data products—one of the hidden bottlenecks in AI. 

 In a matter of months, with help from domain experts beyond SAP Labs India, the proof-of-concept (PoC) became the Data Product Creation Agent. 

 The speed of development was astonishing, says Leena Kharti, development manager for the team. Kharti, who has worked in development for 16 years, attributes this to the mindset shift in her team. “We got into the habit of thinking differently: today there’s a blocker, so let’s work on something else that moves us forward. In AI, speed is a feature, and that mindset made all the difference,” she says. 

 The same spirit of innovation extends beyond SAP Labs India’s own teams to the wider network of founders, engineers, and emerging technology firms around them—and the ideas it generates. 

 India’s startup ecosystem—the third largest in the world—has become a powerful source of innovation, complementing the country’s deep engineering talent and entrepreneurial culture. This offers SAP Labs India a valuable pipeline of new ideas, technologies, and partnerships that can help shape the next generation of enterprise software. 

 To tap into that energy, SAP Labs India launched the SAP Startup Studio program in Bengaluru in June 2026. The six-month accelerator program offers selected startups the opportunity to co-create enterprise-ready solutions with SAP teams and scale through SAP’s global ecosystem. 

 This year’s cohort included ANSCER Robotics, Pulse Energy, and QNu Labs, whose work spans enterprise AI, robotics, industrial intelligence, and quantum-safe technologies. 

 While the focus areas of this year’s cohort differ, the program’s goal is the same: to turn emerging technologies into practical business solutions. This provides SAP an early window into innovations that could help define the future of the Autonomous Enterprise. 

 “ India has all the ingredients to win in AI” 

 India has an outstanding talent pipeline with more than 2.5 million STEM graduates in 2026 and one of the world’s most dynamic startup ecosystems. Combined with SAP Labs India’s growing role in innovations such as Joule and agentic AI, these strengths are shaping the solutions SAP delivers to customers worldwide. 

 As SAP advances its vision of the Autonomous Enterprise, the importance of SAP Labs India lies not simply in its size but in its influence on what SAP ships to its global customer base. 

 “India has all the ingredients required to win in AI,” says CEO of SAP SE Christian Klein. “First, the quality of technical talent and universities is extremely strong. Second, India is investing heavily in building the infrastructure that AI ecosystems need. And third, it’s a country that is pro-business with a strong focus on becoming an even better place to invest.”

3.summary: Introduces the Destination Job type in SAP Job Scheduling Service on BTP, which calls applications outside the scheduler's CF space or Kyma namespace by resolving a named destination through the SAP Destination service. The post argues this removes the need for an intermediary proxy service that relays scheduled calls. It lists prerequisites, the supported destination authentication methods, and a high-level execution flow. The excerpt ends just before the dashboard creation steps, so the actual configuration is not covered.
key_points: Destination Jobs only accept destinations created in the SAP Destination service; ad hoc or hardcoded URLs are not supported.
The job type targets applications outside the calling CF space or Kyma namespace, replacing custom relay code.
Prerequisites: a Job Scheduling Service instance, a Destination service instance in the same subaccount, and a configured destination.
Dashboard access requires SpaceDeveloper (CF) or SAP_Job_Scheduling_Service_Admin (Kyma).

Supported authentication types include No Auth, Basic, Client Certificate, OAuth2 Client Credentials/JWT Bearer/SAML Bearer/User Token Exchange, and Principal Propagation (which needs the Connectivity service).
The post's flow diagram is ambiguous about which component actually performs the outbound call after the Destination service returns connection details.
technical_details: SAP Job Scheduling Service, job type 'Destination Job' (new)
SAP Destination service instance in the same BTP subaccount
Roles: SpaceDeveloper (Cloud Foundry), SAP_Job_Scheduling_Service_Admin (Kyma)

Destination auth methods: No Authentication, Basic, Client Certificate (mTLS), OAuth2 Client Credentials, OAuth2 JWT Bearer, OAuth2 SAML Bearer Assertion, OAuth2 User Token Exchange, Principal Propagation
Connectivity service for on-premise and Principal Propagation scenarios
Existing job types for comparison: HTTP Jobs (sync/async action endpoint) and CF Task Jobs
No API payloads, REST calls, or dashboard screens shown in the excerpt
3.why_it_matters: It removes a common pattern where teams wrote a proxy app just to forward scheduled calls to external systems. Centralising connectivity and credentials in the Destination service keeps secrets out of job code and reuses existing destination governance.
3.teaching_angle: Use it to contrast HTTP Jobs (internal endpoints) with Destination Jobs, and to discuss why destination-based connectivity and principal propagation matter for secured outbound calls. Ask students to verify from the official docs which component performs the call and how run logs report failures, since the post leaves that unclear.

5.summary: Describes an architecture for moving large master or transactional datasets using SAP Integration Suite, JMS queues, and page-based source API calls. A scheduler enqueues a trigger, a planning step computes page count and creates one job message per page, and execution flows consume those messages and deliver batches to the target through pipeline outbound steps. It is a conceptual blueprint with no iFlow configuration, queue names, retry settings, or code. Most of the reliability and parallelism claims are asserted rather than shown.
key_points: Scheduler triggers a message into an initial JMS queue for persistence and retry.
Planning step reads the total record count and creates one JMS job message per page (example: 1,000,000 records / 10,000 page size = 100 jobs).
Each job calls the source API with page number and page size, then forwards the batch to the target.
Reliability is attributed to JMS persistence and to pipeline outbound steps' retry behaviour, with no settings given.
Parallel execution is claimed as a benefit but no concurrency configuration is described.
Offset-style paging over a date range is used without addressing how changing source data could cause missed or duplicated records.
technical_details: SAP Integration Suite, Cloud Integration pipeline flows (as named in the post)
JMS queues for planning and execution stages
Pipeline Generic Step 06 (Outbound Processing) and Step 08 (XI Outbound Processing), as named by the author; their behaviour is not documented in the post
Source API contract: record count endpoint plus paged retrieval by page number, page size and date range
Example arithmetic: 1,000,000 records at 10,000 per page = 100 jobs
No concurrency, retry count, or dead-letter settings given
5.why_it_matters: Large-volume sync is a frequent integration task, and splitting work into page-level JMS messages is a reasonable pattern. However, the post gives a diagram-level design without the concrete settings a team would need to implement and operate it.
5.teaching_angle: Good discussion piece on decomposing bulk sync into idempotent page jobs. Students should be asked what happens with duplicate delivery on retry, how to make page jobs idempotent, and whether offset paging is stable when source data changes during the run.

6.summary: Part 1 of a series on CDS view extensions in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, using a business scenario (Joule and SAC cannot see a Z-table field versus a standard field not yet released) to frame the difference between missing extensions and missing release. It explains the RISE upgrade model, why activation errors during SUM block transports, and how the C1 release contract and EXTEND VIEW ENTITY protect extensions. It ends mid-way through the A–D clean core classification table, so the later levels and examples are not visible.
key_points: CDS view extensions are created with EXTEND VIEW ENTITY in ADT and sit in the Developer In-App tier.
Extending a C1-released view is presented as Level A (ABAP Cloud compliant, upgrade-safe); extending unreleased views or using Z-copies has no upgrade contract.
In a system on the ABAP Cloud language version, references to unreleased objects are a build failure, not a warning.
SUM runs ABAP activation checks against customer-namespace objects in the development system; failures block the transport chain.
The author recommends running ATC against the extension estate before each Feature Pack Stack.
Release rhythm described: base release every two years (2023, 2025, 2027), FPS every six months, seven years mainstream maintenance per base release.

EXTEND VIEW ENTITY (CDS view extension) in ABAP Development Tools (ADT)
C1-released views and C0/C1 release contracts
ABAP Cloud language version compile-time rejection of unreleased objects

deep_dives.title: Extending CDS views safely: EXTEND VIEW ENTITY and C1 release contracts
deep_dives.explanation:
In S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, CDS view extensions are created in ADT with `EXTEND VIEW ENTITY`. The source describes the key question as whether the base view is released with a C1 contract. Extending a C1-released view is classed as Level A (ABAP Cloud compliant, upgrade-safe). Extending an unreleased view, or copying it into a Z-view, has no upgrade contract, so SAP can change the underlying object without regard to your extension.

With the ABAP Cloud language version, referencing an unreleased object is a build failure, not a warning. This matters for upgrades: SUM runs ABAP activation checks against customer-namespace objects in the development system, and failures block the transport chain. The author recommends running ATC over the extension estate before each Feature Pack Stack, which is a cheap way to find problems early.

The post has no code, so here is the shape to teach (a sketch, not from the post): an `extend view entity I_Xyz with { ... }` in a DDLX/DDL source, adding a field from a Z-table via association or join. Before writing it, open the base view in ADT and check its release state (C0/C1). The post also separates two problems that look alike: a missing extension (your Z field is not exposed) and a missing release (the standard field exists but is not released for use).

The excerpt ends before Levels B–D, so do not teach the full classification from this post alone.

deep_dives.title: Dropping parent records by deep predicate in CPI XSLT
deep_dives.explanation:
The poster uses `<xsl:mode on-no-match="shallow-copy"/>`, which copies everything unless a more specific template matches. To remove a whole record, match the record itself rather than the leaf. A template such as `<xsl:template match="EmpEmployment[jobInfoNav/EmpJob/customString15Nav/cust_EC_GL_GlobalEmploymentType/externalCode = '1']"/>` with an empty body suppresses the node and its subtree. This is a suggested direction, not confirmed in the post.

The shallow-copy rule does not run for that node because the explicit template is chosen for it and produces nothing. Keep the predicate relative to the repeating record. The sample XML seems to wrap two EmpEmployment elements inside another EmpEmployment, so check whether that wrapper is real. If it is, a predicate on the outer element could behave unexpectedly, for example by matching if any descendant record has code 1.

Hardening options: `normalize-space(externalCode) = '1'` to tolerate whitespace. For very large files, streamable XSLT (`xsl:mode streamable="yes"`) may help, but descendant predicates can break streamability rules, so test it. Nothing in the post benchmarks any approach.
key_concepts: Template matching on the repeating record

deep_dives.title: BTP Destination Jobs versus HTTP Jobs
deep_dives.explanation:
HTTP Jobs call an action endpoint of an app bound to the scheduler (sync or async). Destination Jobs target applications outside the scheduler's CF space or Kyma namespace, via a destination defined in the SAP Destination service in the same subaccount. Hardcoded or ad hoc URLs are rejected, so connectivity and credentials stay under destination governance.

The post lists the supported authentication types: No Auth, Basic, Client Certificate, OAuth2 Client Credentials, JWT Bearer, SAML Bearer, User Token Exchange, and Principal Propagation, which needs the Connectivity service. For on-premise targets the Connectivity service is also involved.

Open points: the post's diagram does not make clear which component performs the outbound call after the Destination service returns connection details, and the excerpt omits the dashboard steps and API payloads. Confirm both in SAP documentation, along with how run logs show failures, before designing around it.

interview_questions.question: Why does choosing a C1-released CDS view matter when extending in S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition?
interview_questions.answer: A C1 release contract means SAP commits to keeping the view's interface stable across upgrades. Extending a released view with EXTEND VIEW ENTITY is therefore upgrade-safe and ABAP Cloud compliant. Extending an unreleased view, or copying it into a Z-view, carries no such contract, so an upgrade can change or remove underlying objects. With the ABAP Cloud language version, referencing unreleased objects is a compile error, not a warning. During upgrades, SUM runs activation checks on customer-namespace objects in the development system, and failures block the transport chain. Running ATC over the extension estate before each Feature Pack Stack catches these early.

interview_questions.question: In CPI XSLT with an identity (shallow-copy) transform, how do you remove an entire parent record when a deeply nested child has a specific value?
interview_questions.answer: Set `xsl:mode on-no-match="shallow-copy"` so everything is copied by default. Then add a template that matches the repeating record with a predicate walking down to the value, for example `EmpEmployment[jobInfoNav/EmpJob/.../externalCode = '1']`, and give it an empty body. That explicit template is selected for the node and emits nothing, so the record and its subtree are dropped. The match must target the repeating record, not a wrapper or the leaf, so check the XML structure. You can harden the predicate with `normalize-space()`. For very large payloads, streamable mode may help, but descendant predicates can limit streamability, so test it rather than assume.

interview_questions.question: You design a large-volume sync as page-per-message jobs on JMS. What reliability issues must you address?
interview_questions.answer: Retries and redelivery mean a page job can run more than once, so each page must be idempotent at the target, for example via upsert on a business key or a deduplication key per page. Offset paging is unstable if source data changes during the run, which can cause missed or duplicated records. Prefer a stable cursor, a snapshot timestamp, or a key-based range. You also need explicit retry limits, dead-letter handling, and concurrency settings, none of which the source post specifies. Finally, add monitoring for page counts and completion so a partial run is detectable.
